in_hebrew.name: ג'רל
in_hebrew.meaning: יהוה יורד, משפט אלוהים, או שופט אלוהים
in_hebrew.long_meaning: השם ג'רל עשוי להיות קשור לשורשים עבריים שמשמעותם 'יהוה יורד' או 'משפט אלוהים'. הוא עשוי להיות גם שינוי של השם העברי 'געראל' שמשמעותו 'שופט אלוהים' או 'אלוהים הוא השופט'. השם נמצא בשימוש במסגרת השמות הנוצריים ומופיע בקרב קהילות יהודיות ונוצריות כאחד.

in_greek.name: Γιάρελ
in_greek.meaning: Κυρίου είναι η κρίσις, ή Κύριος ο δικαστής
in_greek.long_meaning: Το όνομα Γιάρελ πιθανόν να συνδέεται με εβραϊκές ρίζες που σημαίνουν 'Κυρίου είναι η κρίσις' ή 'Κύριος ο δικαστής'. Μπορεί να είναι μια παραλλαγή του εβραϊκού ονόματος 'Γκεραλ' που σημαίνει 'ο Θεός είναι ο δικαστής'. Το όνομα απαντάται στην παράδοση των χριστιανικών ονομάτων και συναντάται τόσο σε εβραϊκές όσο και σε χριστιανικές κοινότητες.

In battles, the outcome was often determined by God's intervention. The name Jarel may have been given to a warrior or leader who was believed to have divine protection and the power to bring down enemies.
data.spiritual_significance: For Christians, the name Jarel can represent the belief in God's sovereignty and divine intervention in one's life. It can serve as a reminder that God is in control and that He ultimately decides the outcome of every situation. The name can also inspire courage and confidence in the face of challenges or trials, knowing that God is with us and will bring us through.
data.spiritual_symbolism: The name Jarel is believed to derive from the Hebrew "Yariel", meaning "God will teach". This name signifies a deep connection to spiritual wisdom and a strong foundation in faith.

historical_references.reference: Jarel, son of Eleazar, was a descendant of the priestly lineage of Abijah in the Southern Kingdom of Judah during the reign of King Jehoshaphat (873-848 BC). He is mentioned in the genealogy of the priestly lineage in 1 Chronicles 24:14.
historical_references.context: Southern Kingdom of Judah, priestly lineage of Abijah

historical_references.reference: Jarel, a chronicler and a member of the minor prophets, is believed to have lived during the Babylonian captivity (586-539 BC) and wrote the book of Lamentations. He is mentioned in the 'Prose Introduction' to the book as one of the three 'Sibyls' who prophesied about Jerusalem's destruction and lamented its desolation.
historical_references.context: Babylonian captivity, wrote the book of Lamentations
